newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar steady at Tokyo noon after erasing gains.
newsitem.headline: Dollar steady at Tokyo noon after erasing gains.

text.p: 0300 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0300 GMT
The dollar was flat with its Thursday New York close level at the Tokyo midday on Friday, after giving up earlier gains to nearly 115 yen.

Selling from a variety of operators and lingering fears of a renewed dollar fall capped the early gains, but the downside was supported after Thursday's remarks from Japanese and U.S. officials who downplayed the issue of Japan's trade surplus.
The dollar rose as high as 114.93 yen, partly due to speculative purchases by Japanese trading houses, dealers said.
But the gains were soon erased due to talk of selling from U.S. hedge funds, Japanese exporters and Asian central banks. Heavier selling interest was also detected above 115 yen.
Subsequent activity was subdued ahead of the weekend and the downside was also supported by talk of bids from Japanese public investors around 113.80 yen, they said.
"Operators, including those who reaped profits or made big losses due to the large fluctuation on Thursday, are basically willing to take a rest for today," said a bank dealer.

The dollar moved more than 4-1/2 yen in the Tokyo session on Thursday after remarks by senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara that recent concern over Japan's growing trade surplus was overdone.

In New York on Thursday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin repeated recent comments that a "sustained" rise in Japan's trade surplus could hurt global growth and spark a protectionist backlash in the U.S.
He said, however, that there was no sign yet that growth in Japan's trade surplus will be sustained and that currency rates will never be used as a tool to manipulate international trade.
The remarks on Thursday by Japanese authorities showed that they did not want to see the dollar below 110 yen, said a senior Japanese bank dealer.
"Personally, as a dealer, I wanted to see the dollar fall below 110 yen, but the Japanese government showed strong determination to protect that level," he added.
He said a dollar decline below 110 yen would have paved the way for large dollar losses by sparking stop-loss sell orders.
Such a decline would also cause heavy losses to some financially weak Japanese insurers and the Finance Ministry did not want to see them in deeper trouble, he added.
"So there may even be a chance of BOJ dollar-buying intervention if the dollar looks like it will fall below that point again," the dealer said.
Tokyo dealers were divided over the direction of the dollar, with some dealers still expecting it to fall to 110 yen due to left-over selling pressure on rallies.

Meanwhile, the dollar was likely to gain against the mark as hopes grew that EU countries would soon agree on the budget deficit stability pact imposing fiscal discipline after they join economic and monetary union.
--Tatsuo Ito, Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-3432-1396
